summary: Give the Hydroelectric power calculator the cross-sectional area, the head, the water density and the gravitational acceleration and it returns flow discharge. That makes it useful for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Hydroelectric power calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hydroelectric power calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports flow discharge in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the turbine type); then you type in the cross-sectional area, the head, the water density and the gravitational acceleration.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as hydroelectric dam, "Run-of-river" installation and tidal power turbine. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms per cubic meter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second squared. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilowatts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in /year.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hydroelectric power calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Flow discharge=power output ÷ (efficiency × gravitational acceleration × head × water density)
Flow discharge=cross-sectional area × flow velocity
Power output=(1 ÷ 2) × flow discharge × efficiency × (flow velocity ^ 2) × water density
Tariff=(1 ÷ 24) × revenue ÷ (operating days × power output)
Revenue=24 × operating days × power output × tariff
Mass flow rate=flow discharge × water density

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hydroelectric power calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the cross-sectional area, the head and the water density — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hydroelectric power calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns flow discharge, derived from the cross-sectional area, the head and the water density. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hydroelectric power calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cross-sectional area, the head, the water density and the gravitational acceleration, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cross-sectional area in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cross-sectional area opens in square meters and the chip beside it offers 24 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Hydroelectric power calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
